rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (lines 405-413), Example 5.5 (line 439-440)
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Derivation (steps written out): for f = mu1/sigma1 - mu2/sigma2 the delta method uses the gradient (1/sigma1, -1/sigma2, -mu1/(2 sigma1^3), mu2/(2 sigma2^3)) with respect to (mean1, mean2, var1, var2). Under iid bivariate normal returns with unit variances and correlation rho, the covariance of the moments is Var(mean_i) = 1, Cov(mean1, mean2) = rho, Var(var_i-hat) = 2, Cov(var1-hat, var2-hat) = 2 rho^2, and zero between means and variances (odd moments vanish). Substituting gives V = 2 - 2 rho + (mu1^2 + mu2^2)/2 - rho^2 mu1 mu2, which is formula (5) with mu_i = SR_i. Numerical check (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify59h-L07-L08/r26/derive_ex55_out.txt, F): the gradient [1, -1, -0.03, 0.02] and V = 0.1004340000 at (0.06, 0.04, 0.95), equal to formula (5) = 0.1004340000. Monte Carlo (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify59h-L07-L08/r26/ex55_mc_and_lab_formula_out.txt, part b): 200,000 replicates of T = 1260 jointly normal daily returns with rho = 0.95: (T-1) Var(SR1-SR2) = 0.10051 with Monte Carlo SE 0.00032, i.e. 0.24 SE above 0.100434 (finite-sample term T/(T-1)). The page's use of T-1 = 1259 is the convention of Definition 5.3 (line 420). PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5, T span (line 272): 'The luck, the expected maximum of the nulls, cannot fall as N grows, because adding a null can only raise the maximum; for standard normal null statistics with any joint law it is at most sqrt(2 ln N) (Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. Monotonicity: with N+1 nulls the maximum is the pointwise maximum over N nulls and one more variable, so it is at least the N-null maximum for every outcome, and its expectation cannot fall. Bound: for any joint law of Z_1..Z_N standard normal, e^{lambda E max Z_n} <= E e^{lambda max Z_n} (Jensen) <= sum_n E e^{lambda Z_n} = N e^{lambda^2/2}, so E max Z_n <= ln N / lambda + lambda/2 for every lambda > 0; lambda = sqrt(2 ln N) gives sqrt(2 ln N). The statement matches Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82), whose scope is 'any joint distribution', and the L08 claim uses no wider scope. The index is the page's N (configurations), and the claim uses the N-1 nulls, with sqrt(2 ln(N-1)) <= sqrt(2 ln N). Concept link to L01 def-expected-maximum-sharpe exists (check_dag PASS). Card S7-c227 now covers it (L08-sec5-expected-max-card-gap). rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Claim: adding a null trial cannot raise the probability that a genuine configuration wins in sample, whatever the joint law. Proof (re-derived): let X0 be the genuine in-sample statistic and M_k the maximum of k null statistics. The winning event with k nulls is {X0 > M_k}; adding a null Y gives {X0 > max(M_k, Y)}, which is contained in {X0 > M_k}, so its probability cannot exceed the earlier one. No independence or distributional assumption is used. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): T span 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite, sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) -> N(0,1), by the CLT for mu-hat, the LLN for sigma-hat and Slutsky's lemma'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Derivation re-checked step by step. (i) SR-hat = mu-hat/sigma-hat, so sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) is an identity. (ii) With iid returns, mean mu = SR sigma = 0 and finite variance sigma^2, the CLT gives sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma -> N(0,1). (iii) sigma-hat^2 = (1/(T-1)) sum (r - r-bar)^2 -> sigma^2 in probability by the LLN applied to r^2 (finite since E r^2 < infinity) and r-bar -> 0; so sigma/sigma-hat -> 1 in probability (the divisor T or T-1 does not matter). (iv) Slutsky gives the limit N(0,1). Nothing beyond finite variance is used. Numerical spot check (scratch num_checks.py, 20000 replications): Student t with 3 df scaled to unit variance, SR = 0: P(z <= -1.6449) = 0.0513 / 0.0502 / 0.0502 and P(z <= 1.6449) = 0.9505 / 0.9500 / 0.9506 at T = 250 / 1000 / 4000 (N(0,1): 0.05 and 0.95); sd(z) = 1.007 / 1.001 / 0.992. The fourth moment is infinite there, so the check is of the claim's sufficiency. Grade T is right (proved on the page). The iid standing assumption is the section 1 assumption ('keep independence'). Attribution (VERIFIER 2.1): the publisher abstract of Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu, The Journal of Computational Finance 20(4) (first published 19 Sep 2016; DOI 10.21314/JCF.2016.322), read on Risk.net with curl -sSL https://www.risk.net/node/2471206 (HTTP 200, 128,762 bytes; final URL https://www.risk.net/journal-of-computational-finance/2471206/the-probability-of-backtest-overfitting). It reads: 'We propose a general framework to assess the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) ... we call these implementations combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV). We show that CSCV produces reasonable estimates of PBO for several useful examples.' The 'Need to know' summary reads: 'Results indicate that CSCV provides reasonable estimates of PBO, with relatively small errors.' The span's claim is what the abstract shows: CSCV is introduced as one way to estimate PBO, and the reasonable estimates are for 'several useful examples' that are the authors' own test cases. Scope is correct. Crossref (curl https://api.crossref.org/works/10.21314/jcf.2016.322) carries no abstract; its title, authors and year match the registry record. Grade: C is correct under BLUEPRINT §3 (single-study evidence from the authors' own examples; the venue is peer-reviewed but nothing replicates the result). Counter-evidence: no named published source contests it (row counter-bailey2016probability). The registry-scoped sentence 'No independent study in the registry has yet evaluated its accuracy' is true: a title scan of references/references.json (557 entries; pattern backtest|overfit|PBO|CSCV|combinatorial|selection bias|data snooping|cross-validation) returns 11 titles, none of which names CSCV. Apart from the source of the claim itself (bailey2016probability, which reports the authors' own examples), none of the 11 evaluates CSCV's estimates (bailey2014deflated, bailey2014pseudo, harvey2015backtesting, romano2005stepwise, white2000reality and others are about selection or snooping, not CSCV). Result: PASS.

rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Search from scratch at f14987f (VERIFIER 2.3; BUILDER 5). (1) Citing works: curl https://api.opencitations.net/index/v2/citations/doi:10.21314/jcf.2016.322 returned HTTP 200 with 43 citing entries (41 DOIs, 2 arXiv IDs: 2512.22476, 2602.11020). (2) Titles and abstracts: Crossref (https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>) for 41 DOIs and DataCite (https://api.datacite.org/dois/10.48550/arXiv.<id>) for the 2 arXiv IDs; 41 records returned. Two Crossref lookups (10.1016/j.knosys.2024.111630; 10.2139/ssrn.3044740) answered HTTP 429; after a 35 s wait both returned HTTP 200 (the first is 'On the design of searching algorithm for parameter plateau in quantitative trading strategies using particle swarm optimization', Knowledge-Based Systems 2024; the second is 'How Hard Is It to Pick the Right Model?', Aparicio and López de Prado, SSRN 2017; neither has a Crossref abstract, and neither concerns CSCV). 17 of the 43 records carry abstracts. (3) Screen: backtest|overfit|PBO|CSCV|cross-validation|combinatorial|out-of-sample|selection bias|data snooping|multiple test over titles and abstracts (scratch citing_records.json). Hits: AutoQuant (arXiv 2512.22476, 2025), LSTM in Algorithmic Investment Strategies (10.3390/s22030917), Statistical Overfitting and Backtest Performance (10.2139/ssrn.2507040, the same four authors' framework), A Bayesian Approach to Measurement of Backtest Overfitting (10.3390/risks9010018), Portfolio Optimization Efficiency Test Considering Data Snooping Bias (10.2478/bsrj-2020-0016), Determining Optimal Trading Rules Without Backtesting (10.2139/ssrn.2658641), Uncovering feature interdependencies (10.1038/s41598-021-88571-3), Differential Effects of Buy and Sell Rules (10.2139/ssrn.2922485), Illegitimate Science (10.2139/ssrn.2599105), Backtesting (10.2139/ssrn.2345489). (4) Candidate read: Arian, Norouzi Mobarekeh and Seco, Knowledge-Based Systems 305, article 112477 (doi 10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112477; Crossref issued 2024-12; no Crossref abstract; the publisher page was not requested in this round, and round 18 recorded HTTP 403 from it). Its SSRN working paper with the same title and authors, 10.2139/ssrn.4686376, was read through curl https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.4686376 (field abstract). The decisive sentences: 'Through our analysis, we unveil the marked superiority of the Combinatorial Purged (CPCV) method in mitigating overfitting risks, outperforming traditional methods like K-Fold, Purged K-Fold, and especially Walk-Forward, as evidenced by its lower Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) and superior Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) Test Statistic.' and 'Our investigation utilizes a Synthetic Controlled Environment incorporating advanced models like the Heston Stochastic Volatility, Merton Jump Diffusion, and Drift-Burst Hypothesis, alongside regime-switching models.' Answer to the decisive question (does it evaluate CSCV's estimates of PBO?): no. CSCV is not among the compared methods; PBO is the outcome used to rank CPCV, K-Fold, Purged K-Fold and Walk-Forward; the abstract says nothing about the accuracy of CSCV's or PBO's estimates. Second SSRN record 10.2139/ssrn.4778909 (same title) has no abstract (Crossref). The published KBS text was not read, so the published version could differ. (5) Others read: Risks 9(1) 18 (2021), Crossref abstract: 'Standard statistical techniques to prevent model overfitting such as out-sample backtesting turn out to be unreliable in situations when the selection is based on results of too many models tested on the holdout sample.' and 'We propose a consistent Bayesian approach ...'; it does not name CSCV or assess CSCV's estimates; MDPI full text HTTP 403 (not read). AutoQuant (arXiv 2512.22476, DataCite abstract): a configuration-selection pipeline for cryptocurrency perpetual futures; it does not evaluate CSCV. SSRN 2507040 is the same authors' framework paper (not independent). SSRN 2745220 ('All that Glitters Is Not Gold', 2016) has no Crossref abstract and was not read. (6) WebSearch (2 queries: 'combinatorially symmetric cross-validation probability of backtest overfitting accuracy independent evaluation simulation'; 'Bailey Borwein Lopez de Prado Zhu probability of backtest overfitting CSCV critique bias estimator'): no independent accuracy evaluation of CSCV appeared; the results repeat the JCF abstract, and a 2014 critique is by the same four authors (registry bailey2014pseudo). (7) OpenAlex: one works lookup (curl https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.21314/jcf.2016.322) returned HTTP 200, not the HTTP 429 the brief expected; OpenAlex was not used for the citing-work list (OpenCitations was). Conclusion: no named published source contests CSCV's estimates in the authors' test cases, and the one 2024 comparison that could have does not evaluate CSCV. The page need not change. Result: PASS (BUILDER 5; VERIFIER 2.3: the search, its counts and what was read are recorded above).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html line 521 (Lab 4 interpretation, part 3): 'At T_beta the first-order mean of the statistic is sqrt(T_beta - 1) SR/sqrt(b(SR)) = sqrt(914) x 0.09/sqrt(1.1962) = 2.488'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Derivation written out. Z_T = SR-hat sqrt(T-1)/sqrt(b-hat) is the statistic inside formula (2) (Remark 2.9). At the true moments its first-order mean is sqrt(T-1) SR/sqrt(b(SR)), with b(SR) = 1 - gamma3 SR + (gamma4 - 1)/4 SR^2; for the lab's mirrored exponential shock (gamma3 = -2, raw gamma4 = 9) b(SR) = 1 + 2 SR + 2 SR^2. At T_beta = 915: sqrt(914) x 0.09 / sqrt(1.1962) = 2.487790 (scratch l07_line521_check.out, line (A)), which rounds to the page's 2.488. Numerical spot-check (scratch l07_line521_check.py, section F): 400,000 replications of the lab's Part 3 data-generating process at n = 915 (independent seed 20261020; statistic formed from the sample moments as in the lab): mean(Z) = 2.4974 (s.e. 0.0015). The first-order value is 0.0096 lower, about 6.6 standard errors, the order-1/T finite-sample correction that the word 'first-order' covers. Result: PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html line 521: 'b(SR) = 1 + 2SR + 2SR^2', 'b(0.09)' bracket 1.1962, 'b'(SR)' and 'first-order standard deviation ... = 0.91' (sentence 3 of the interpretation) and '0.911' in the prediction
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: b(0.09) = 1 + 2(0.09) + 2(0.09)^2 = 1.1962; b'(SR) = 2 + 4 SR = 2.36 (both on the page). First-order standard deviation of the statistic: 1 - SR b'(SR)/(2 b) = 1 - 0.2124/2.3924 = 0.911219, which rounds to 0.911 (the first sentence prints 0.91). Derivation: Var(SR-hat) is about b/(T-1), and d/dSR-hat [SR-hat/sqrt(b(SR-hat))] = (1/sqrt(b))(1 - SR-hat b'/(2b)), so Var(Z) is about (1 - SR b'/(2b))^2. Spot-check (scratch l07_line521_check.out, section F): the 400,000-replication sd(Z) = 0.9168 (s.e. about 0.0010), against 0.9112 at first order. The claim that the plug-in standard error rises with SR-hat and so narrows the spread is consistent: b increases in SR-hat because gamma3 < 0, and the sd is below 1. Result: PASS.

Title 'Endogeneity and moments in time series momentum’s predictability test'; authors Lei Jiang, Liang Peng, Zhongling Qin, Bingduo Yang; The Annals of Applied Statistics 19(1), 701–719; issued 2025-03-01; publisher Institute of Mathematical Statistics. Registry record (references/references.json, entry added at 3e8fe81) gives the same title, authors, year, container, volume 19, issue 1, pages 701-719 and publisher; verify_refs checks in r23-cmd-verify_refs-unit-S7 and r23-cmd-verify_refs-offline pass. Abstract, verbatim from Crossref (JATS tags removed): 'The predictability test is critical in developing momentum trading strategies. In time-series momentum (TSM) tests via linear predictive regressions, the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions because of endogeneity and a lack of enough finite moments. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test that features a model of the error correlations, weighted least squares estimation, and the random weighted bootstrap method. Simulations confirm its accurate size and good power. Empirically, we revisit the evidence in (J. Financ. Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794) and find that the TSM predictability detected by the new test is much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests.' Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794)', which is Huang, Li, Wang and Zhou (registry huang2020time: JFE 135(3) 774–794, the same volume and pages); 'a test that corrects the size distortions of the classical and Newey–West t-tests' paraphrases 'the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions ... To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test ... Simulations confirm its accurate size'. 'corrects' is a fair one-word gloss of 'tackle' plus the authors' simulated 'accurate size'; the simulation basis is the paper's own, so it sits under the B grade of the span; 'much more widespread than the Newey–West tests detect' is 'much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests'.
